articles.label: ACCOUNTABILITY
articles.headline: Escambia County's $2.3M IT Contract Renewed Without Bid Process
articles.dek: County commissioners quietly extended a consulting agreement last week that critics say should have gone to competitive bidding. The vendor has donated to three sitting commissioners.
brief: Escambia County commissioners voted 4-1 to extend a $2.3 million IT consulting contract with Emerald Coast Technology Solutions without opening the agreement to competitive bids.
Campaign finance records show the vendor has donated a combined $14,500 to three of the four commissioners who voted yes since 2022.
County purchasing policy requires competitive bidding for contracts over $50,000, but administrators used a renewal clause in the original 2021 agreement to bypass the requirement.
articles.body:
The agenda item appeared on page 47 of the May 19 consent calendar. No discussion. No public comment. The vote took less than ten seconds.

With that, Escambia County commissioners extended a $2.3 million information technology consulting contract for another three years.

The vendor, Emerald Coast Technology Solutions, has held the county's IT modernization contract since 2021. The Pensacola-based firm has also donated $14,500 to the campaigns of three commissioners who voted to approve the extension: Jeff Bergosh, Mike Kohler, and Steven Barry.

Commissioner Lumon May cast the lone no vote. Commissioner Francesca Mathis was absent.

"I don't like the optics," May said in an interview Thursday. "When you've got a vendor giving money to the people deciding whether to keep paying them, you need to at least put it out to bid. Let the public see that we're getting the best deal."

The Consent Calendar

County consent calendars bundle routine items—equipment purchases, grant acceptances, contract renewals—into a single vote. Commissioners can pull individual items for separate discussion, but they rarely do.

The IT contract renewal appeared as item 47C on a 63-item consent agenda. The item description read: "Renewal of Agreement 2021-IT-0094 with Emerald Coast Technology Solutions for Information Technology Consulting Services."

No dollar figure appeared in the description. To find the $2.3 million total, a resident would need to pull the backup documentation from the county's online agenda system, navigate to attachment 47C-1, and scroll to page four of the renewal amendment.

The Flightline obtained the full contract file through a public records request submitted May 20.

The Donation Trail

Campaign finance records filed with the Escambia County Supervisor of Elections show Emerald Coast Technology Solutions and its principals have contributed to local campaigns since at least 2018.

Since 2022, when the current IT contract was already in effect:

  • Commissioner Bergosh received $6,000 across four donations from ECTS and company president David Holbrook
  • Commissioner Kohler received $5,000 across three donations
  • Commissioner Barry received $3,500 across two donations

All donations fell within legal limits. Florida law caps individual contributions to county commission candidates at $1,000 per election.

Holbrook did not respond to phone messages and an email seeking comment. A receptionist at the company's Airport Boulevard office said Holbrook was traveling and unavailable.

Commissioner Bergosh, reached by phone Friday, said the donations played no role in his vote.

"I've gotten donations from hundreds of people and businesses over the years," Bergosh said. "I don't keep a running tally in my head when I'm voting on agenda items. The IT department recommended the renewal. The work's been satisfactory. That's what I based my vote on."

Commissioners Kohler and Barry did not respond to requests for comment.

The Bidding Question

Escambia County's purchasing policy, last updated in 2019, requires competitive sealed bids for any contract exceeding $50,000. The policy lists several exceptions, including "renewal or extension of existing contracts where renewal terms were established in the original solicitation."

County purchasing director Angela Martinez confirmed the 2021 contract included language allowing up to two three-year renewals at the county's discretion. This is the first renewal.

"The original contract went through full competitive bidding in 2021," Martinez said. "The renewal clause was part of what vendors bid on. Using it now is consistent with policy."

But the 2021 bidding process drew only two submissions, according to procurement records. ECTS won with a bid roughly $400,000 lower than the other applicant, a Jacksonville firm called Coastal Digital Systems.

Coastal Digital did not bid on the original contract and declined to comment on whether they would have competed for a 2026 rebid.

Eric Stevenson, a procurement attorney in Tallahassee who reviewed the contract at The Flightline's request, said the renewal clause is legally permissible but raises questions.

"There's nothing illegal here," Stevenson said. "But best practice in 2026, after five years of market changes, would be to test the market again. IT consulting rates have shifted significantly. The county might be leaving money on the table."

What the Contract Covers

The ECTS agreement covers what the county calls its "digital transformation initiative"—an ongoing effort to modernize aging software systems, improve cybersecurity, and migrate records to cloud storage.

Under the contract, ECTS provides project management, software implementation support, and staff training. The company does not provide the actual software, which the county purchases separately.

County IT director Robert Finch, in a memo supporting the renewal, wrote that ECTS "has consistently delivered quality work product and maintained positive working relationships with county staff." The memo did not compare ECTS rates to current market alternatives.

Finch did not respond to a request for interview.

The $2.3 million renewal breaks down to roughly $767,000 annually over three years. The original 2021 contract totaled $1.9 million over five years, or $380,000 annually—meaning the per-year cost has more than doubled.

Martinez attributed the increase to expanded scope. "The renewal includes additional cybersecurity services that weren't part of the original contract," she said. She declined to specify which services without a formal public records request.

A Pattern?

The IT contract is not the only recent sole-source or limited-competition agreement to draw scrutiny.

In February, the commission renewed a $1.1 million janitorial services contract with Gulf Coast Building Maintenance—another vendor whose owners have donated to sitting commissioners—using a similar renewal clause.

In 2024, a Pensacola News Journal investigation found that Escambia County used sole-source justifications at nearly twice the rate of similarly sized Florida counties.

Commissioner May said he plans to propose a policy review at the June 2 commission meeting.

"I want to look at whether these multi-year renewal clauses are serving the taxpayers or just making life easier for purchasing staff," May said. "Convenience shouldn't trump competition."

County Administrator Wes Moreno declined to comment on whether he would support policy changes.

The next ECTS contract renewal would come in 2029—one year after the next commission election cycle.

articles.label: Development
articles.headline: Downtown Pensacola's Empty Storefronts Hit 15-Year High as Rent Doubles
articles.dek: Palafox Street landlords are betting on a comeback that hasn't arrived. Small business owners say they're being priced out of a district with fewer customers than 2019.
brief: Vacancy rates in downtown Pensacola's core commercial district have reached 23%, the highest since 2011, according to data from the Downtown Improvement Board.
Average asking rents on Palafox Street have climbed from $18 per square foot in 2019 to $36 per square foot in 2026, even as foot traffic remains below pre-pandemic levels.
At least 14 locally owned businesses have closed or relocated out of downtown since January 2025, citing rent increases and declining sales.
articles.body:
The windows at 21 South Palafox have been papered over for nine months. A faded "For Lease" sign lists a number that goes to voicemail. Next door, another empty storefront. Across the street, a third.

Walk four blocks down Pensacola's main commercial corridor on a Tuesday afternoon and you'll count 11 vacant ground-floor spaces. Some have been empty for over a year. A few still show traces of the businesses that left—a painted logo on brick, holes where a sign once hung.

Downtown Pensacola is experiencing its highest commercial vacancy rate in 15 years. According to data obtained from the Downtown Improvement Board through a public records request, 23% of ground-floor retail and restaurant space in the core district sat empty as of April 2026. That's up from 14% in 2022 and 9% in 2019.

The numbers tell one story. The landlords and tenants fighting over lease terms tell another.

The rent question

Maria Castellanos spent eight years building Lola's, a women's clothing boutique on the 100 block of South Palafox. She closed in February.

"My rent went from $2,400 a month to $4,800," Castellanos said. "Same space. Same foot traffic—actually less foot traffic. I couldn't make the math work anymore."

Her landlord, a Pensacola-based LLC that owns four properties on the block, declined to comment for this story.

Castellanos isn't alone. The Flightline interviewed owners or former owners of 11 downtown businesses that have closed or relocated since January 2025. Nine cited rent increases as a primary factor. The increases ranged from 40% to 120% over previous lease terms.

Commercial real estate data from CoStar Group shows average asking rents on Palafox Street have climbed from $18 per square foot in 2019 to $36 per square foot in 2026. Some premium corner spaces are listed at $45.

Those rates approach what landlords charge in downtown Tampa and exceed averages in Mobile and Biloxi.

"The pricing assumes a customer base that doesn't exist here," said Tom Brennan, a commercial real estate broker with Levin Rinke who has represented downtown tenants for 20 years. "Landlords are pricing for where they want the market to be, not where it is."

The customer gap

Before the pandemic, downtown Pensacola was riding a decade-long revival. The 2019 Downtown Improvement Board annual report celebrated record foot traffic, low vacancies, and a waiting list for retail space.

That momentum stalled in 2020 and never fully returned.

Pedestrian counters installed by the DIB show foot traffic in the core district averaged 12,400 daily visitors in April 2019. In April 2026, the average was 8,900—a 28% decline.

Several factors explain the gap. Office occupancy downtown remains below 60%, according to building managers interviewed by The Flightline. Many professional services firms that once filled second and third floors have shifted to hybrid or remote work permanently. Their employees aren't buying lunch on Palafox anymore.

Cruise ship visits, which brought thousands of day-trippers to the port, ended in 2020 and haven't resumed. The city's agreement with Carnival expired, and negotiations for a new deal have stalled over port infrastructure costs.

And the retail mix has shifted. Several downtown spaces that once held shops now house insurance agencies, law offices, and financial advisors—businesses that serve clients by appointment, not walk-in traffic.

"You can't sustain a retail district when half the ground floors are professional services," Brennan said. "Those businesses don't generate foot traffic. They absorb space."

Who's buying and why

Property records show a significant shift in downtown ownership over the past five years. Between 2021 and 2025, at least 18 commercial properties in the core district changed hands. The buyers include out-of-state investment groups, Florida-based LLCs with no local ties, and a handful of local investors betting on appreciation.

One buyer, a Delaware-registered LLC called Emerald Coast Holdings, acquired three Palafox properties in 2023 for a combined $4.2 million. All three ground-floor spaces are currently vacant. The LLC's registered agent did not respond to requests for comment.

Local broker Rachel Simmons, who represented buyers in several downtown transactions, said many new owners are playing a long game.

"They're not desperate to fill space," Simmons said. "They bought at prices that assume future appreciation. They can afford to wait for the tenant who'll pay what they want."

That patience creates a standoff. Landlords hold out for higher rents. Potential tenants can't afford the asking price. Storefronts sit empty. The vacancy itself becomes a drag on the district's appeal.

"Every empty window makes the next lease harder," said former business owner Castellanos. "People don't want to open in a ghost town."

City Hall's limited options

Pensacola City Council member Allison Patton represents District 6, which includes downtown. She said she's heard from frustrated business owners and residents but acknowledged the city has few tools to address commercial rent pricing.

"We can't tell private property owners what to charge," Patton said. "That's not how this works. What we can do is look at what we control—parking, streetscape, permitting, events—and make sure we're not creating additional barriers."

The city has invested in downtown infrastructure in recent years. A $3.2 million streetscape project completed in 2024 added trees, wider sidewalks, and new lighting to portions of Palafox. The Community Redevelopment Agency continues to offer facade grants and small business incentives.

But the CRA's budget is constrained, and its programs primarily help businesses that already have leases. They don't address the fundamental rent gap.

Downtown Improvement Board Executive Director Curt Morse said the organization is "monitoring the situation" but emphasized that commercial real estate cycles are normal.

"We've seen vacancies rise and fall before," Morse said. "The fundamentals of downtown are still strong. We have a beautiful historic district, proximity to the waterfront, and an engaged community. The market will correct."

He declined to offer a timeline for that correction.

What's still working

Not every block is struggling. The 400 and 500 blocks of South Palafox, closer to the bay, maintain lower vacancy rates and a cluster of established restaurants and bars. Several new businesses have opened in that stretch in the past year, including a wine bar and a vintage furniture store.

The difference, according to multiple brokers, is ownership. Many properties in that stretch are held by long-term local owners who've kept rents relatively stable.

"There's a direct correlation," Brennan said. "The blocks with patient local landlords have tenants. The blocks with aggressive pricing have vacancies."

Gallery Night, the monthly art walk that draws thousands to downtown, continues to pack Palafox on the third Friday of each month. But business owners say the event's impact has diminished as the retail mix has thinned.

"People come for Gallery Night, but there's less for them to buy," said James Whitfield, owner of a downtown art supply store that has occupied the same space for 15 years. "Half the storefronts are empty or closed. They walk around, have a drink, and leave."

Whitfield's rent increased 25% at his last renewal in 2024. He said he's not sure he can absorb another increase when his lease expires next year.

"I've been here since before the revitalization," he said. "I remember when downtown was genuinely struggling. This feels different. This feels like we're pricing ourselves into a different kind of failure."

No easy answers

Commercial vacancy is a lagging indicator. The empty storefronts visible today reflect decisions made months or years ago—leases not renewed, businesses that closed, new owners who set prices the market wouldn't bear.

Whether downtown Pensacola's current vacancy rate represents a temporary correction or the beginning of a longer decline depends on variables no one fully controls: interest rates, remote work trends, tourism patterns, and the calculations of property owners who may be thousands of miles away.

For now, the papered windows remain. The "For Lease" signs multiply. And the people who built businesses on Palafox Street watch from the outside.

"I drive by my old space sometimes," Castellanos said. "Nine months and nobody's moved in. Whatever they're waiting for, it hasn't shown up yet."

articles.label: Local News
articles.headline: Blue Angels Return to Pensacola Beach for First Post-Pandemic Memorial Day Show
articles.dek: An estimated 200,000 visitors are expected to pack the island this weekend. For locals, that means closed bridges, $40 parking, and the annual debate over whether it's worth it.
brief: The Blue Angels will perform their full demonstration over Pensacola Beach Saturday and Sunday, the first Memorial Day weekend show since 2019.
Santa Rosa Island Authority expects 200,000 visitors across the weekend, with beach parking reaching capacity by 8 a.m. both days.
The Bob Sikes Bridge will close to inbound traffic when the island reaches capacity, typically between 9 and 10 a.m.
articles.body:
The first F/A-18 Super Hornet screamed over Casino Beach at 11:47 a.m. Saturday, and Maria Gonzalez felt it in her chest before she heard it. She pressed her hands over her three-year-old daughter's ears and looked up. The jet was already gone, banking hard over Santa Rosa Sound, leaving only a white contrail dissolving into blue sky.

"Every single year," Gonzalez said. She lives in Gulf Breeze and crossed the bridge at 6:30 a.m. to claim a spot near the Pensacola Beach Pier. "You forget how loud they are. Then they come back and you remember."

The Blue Angels returned to Pensacola Beach this weekend for their first Memorial Day air show since 2019. The COVID-19 pandemic canceled the 2020 and 2021 shows. Supply chain delays and runway construction at Naval Air Station Pensacola pushed back the 2022 through 2025 events to July. This year, the team is home for the holiday weekend, and the island is bracing for what officials expect to be the largest crowd in a decade.

The Logistics of 200,000 People on a Barrier Island

Santa Rosa Island Authority Executive Director Paolo Ghio said the agency expects 200,000 visitors across Saturday and Sunday. That number comes from vehicle counts, parking revenue, and surveys conducted at previous shows.

"This is the Super Bowl for Pensacola Beach," Ghio said Friday afternoon, standing in the parking lot behind the Boardwalk. Crews were erecting temporary fencing and positioning portable restrooms. "We've been planning since January."

The island has roughly 3,800 public parking spaces. At $40 per vehicle for event parking—up from $30 in 2019—those spaces generate more than $150,000 per day for the island authority's operating budget. Private lots along Via de Luna Drive were charging $60 to $100 Saturday morning.

By 8:15 a.m. Saturday, the Casino Beach lot was full. By 9:30, Escambia County Sheriff's Office deputies began turning vehicles around at the foot of the Bob Sikes Bridge. The bridge reopened briefly at 11 a.m., closed again at 11:40, and remained closed until 2 p.m.

"If you're not on the island by eight, you're probably not getting on the island," said ECSO Sergeant David Chen, who has worked the air show for nine years. "People get mad. I get it. But there's nowhere to put them."

For Some Locals, the Show Is the Problem

Not everyone on Pensacola Beach was celebrating. At the Sandshaker Lounge on Quietwater Beach, bartender Tommy Reeves poured drinks for a crowd that was half tourists, half regulars who live on the island year-round.

"I love the Blue Angels," Reeves said. "I hate air show weekend." He gestured toward Via de Luna, where traffic had been at a standstill for two hours. "I live on Ariola Drive. It took me forty-five minutes to get to work. That's a mile and a half."

Reeves said he usually leaves the island entirely on air show weekend, staying with family in Cantonment. This year, he couldn't get the time off.

Linda Simmons, who has owned a condo on Portofino Island since 2008, watched the show from her twelfth-floor balcony with binoculars. She did not go down to the beach.

"The crowd is too much," Simmons said. "And honestly, after you've seen it fifteen times, the magic wears off a little." She paused as a formation of four jets roared past, close enough that she could see the pilots' helmets. "Okay, maybe not completely."

The Show Itself

The Blue Angels' demonstration runs approximately 45 minutes. The team flies six F/A-18 Super Hornets, which replaced the older F/A-18 Hornets in 2021. The Super Hornets are larger, louder, and faster. They can exceed 700 miles per hour, though most maneuvers during the beach show are performed at speeds between 300 and 400 miles per hour.

Commanding Officer Captain Brian Kesselring, the team's flight leader and narrator, addressed the crowd over loudspeakers before Saturday's performance.

"This is home," Kesselring said. "We train here. We live here. Our families are in the stands today. There's no crowd we'd rather fly for."

The team is based at NAS Pensacola and practices over the beach and Perdido Key throughout the year. That proximity breeds both familiarity and fatigue. Residents along the flight path hear the jets multiple times per week during training season.

"You get used to it," said Mark Underwood, who lives in the Innerarity Point neighborhood on Perdido Key. "My dog does not get used to it. He hides in the bathtub every time they fly."

Economic Impact and the Annual Debate

Visit Pensacola, the county's tourism marketing agency, estimates the Memorial Day air show generates between $20 million and $25 million in direct visitor spending. Hotels within five miles of the beach were fully booked by mid-April. Vacation rental rates on the island doubled from typical Memorial Day weekend prices, according to data from AirDNA, a short-term rental analytics firm.

The Escambia County Tourist Development Council, which collects a 5% bed tax on accommodations, will release official revenue figures in July.

Whether that economic activity benefits year-round residents is a matter of ongoing debate. Pensacola Beach is an unincorporated community governed by the Santa Rosa Island Authority, which operates under a lease with Escambia County. Permanent residents number fewer than 5,000. On air show weekend, they are outnumbered forty to one.

"The money goes to the hotels and the restaurants," said Jeff Parker, president of the Pensacola Beach Advocates, a resident group. "The traffic and the trash go to us." Parker said the organization has asked the island authority to implement a resident-only vehicle pass for event weekends. The authority has not acted on that request.

Ghio, the island authority director, said the show brings benefits that extend beyond the weekend. "National exposure, brand recognition for Pensacola Beach, and a reminder that this is a military town," he said. "You can't put a dollar figure on that."

Sunday's Forecast and What to Expect

The National Weather Service Pensacola forecast calls for partly cloudy skies Sunday with a 20% chance of afternoon thunderstorms. Show time is noon. If weather delays the performance, it will begin 30 minutes after conditions clear. If conditions do not clear, the show will be canceled; there is no rain date.

Deputies will begin staging at the Bob Sikes Bridge toll plaza at 5 a.m. Ghio recommended arriving before 7 a.m. Visitors who arrive after the bridge closes can watch from Shoreline Park South in Gulf Breeze, though the view is distant and partially obstructed by buildings on the island's sound side.

For Maria Gonzalez, the early wake-up was worth it. Her daughter, Sofia, had fallen asleep on a beach towel by 1 p.m., exhausted from the sun and the noise. Gonzalez sat beside her, watching the last of the crowd filter back toward the parking lots.

"She won't remember this one," Gonzalez said. "But I'll bring her back next year, and the year after that. Eventually it'll stick." She looked up at the empty sky. "That's how it works here. You grow up with the Blue Angels. They're just part of the place."
